opener.heading: Week 19: Mother's Day & Family Love 💐
about: This week points Azlyn at the four people in her own house. She photographs them, feeds them, makes a toy for Kreston, mends what belongs to them and puts clean sheets on their beds. A family is a set of people you do things for, and she is old enough now to be one of the ones doing.

Mother's Day lands on Sunday. Saturday builds toward it, she lays the table for five and guards the plate in the fridge, and Monday winds back down out of it into the button tin and a shoebox of things nobody throws away. The handprint card she paints on Sunday is May's, fifth of this year's twelve, so hold April's sheet up beside it and put both back on the wall.
azlyn: What a frame leaves out. She lines up every shot through a cardboard window first, so choosing one thing means dropping another.
What it takes for two things to be the same. A tin of odds and ends hunted for exact twins, and every near miss argued out with a reason she has to say out loud.
Making something for a particular person. The plate, the card, the cake and Kreston's rattle all get judged on whether they land with the person they were for.
Hand strength with a point to it. Cracking an egg, beating batter until it holds on the fork, pushing wool through a needle eye, pulling a stitch through from her side.
Carrying her own share of the work. A wet laundry basket across the grass, two full watering cans, a pillow shoved into its case.

shopping: An old phone or a digital camera, charged, with last year's photographs cleared off
A cereal box, for the viewfinder
Thick card, letter size or bigger, 12 sheets
One sharp pair of scissors (adult only)
April's and January's handprint sheets, off the wall
One printed photograph for the keepsake box
A large plate or serving dish
Small bowls or saucers, 8 (five for the big plate, two for the button tin, one for the handprint water)
Napkins, or a roll of paper towels
A blunt table knife and a butter knife
A plain sponge cake or a store-bought loaf cake (plain cookies do the same job)
A mixing bowl and a spoon
A fork, a grater (adult only), a frying pan and a spatula
Whatever is on its last day in the fridge: a tired carrot, a zucchini, a cooked potato, the end of the cheese, soft herbs
The button tin, or a jar filled from the odds-and-ends drawer: bottle caps, coins, keys, corks, lids, clothespins, spoons, fabric scraps
A large blunt darning needle, or fabric glue or iron-on patches
A scrap of fabric for a patch
Two or three torn things out of the mending pile, and the soft toy with the split seam
A clean plastic bottle with a screw lid
A low basket or a dishpan
Dish soap and a dish towel

Household objects for Kreston's basket: wooden spoon, metal tablespoon, small saucepan lid, silicone spatula, hairbrush, washcloth, cotton scarf, metal measuring cup, small mixing bowl, tea strainer, wooden coaster
A clothespin bag and 30 clothespins or more
A clothesline dropped to her height, or a clothes airer she can reach over
Clean sheets, duvet covers and pillowcases for every bed
A jam jar for her flowers
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 11 months this week. He stands alone for a second or two before he sits down hard, cruises anything at hip height, and babbles in strings all day. He stops when you start, which is him taking his turn.

days.title: The Family Photographer
days.prepTonight: Cut a postcard-sized rectangle out of a cereal box with a window in the middle of it and leave it on the table, and put the old camera on charge with last year's photographs cleared off it.

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: The Forks and the Water Pitcher

opening.title: The Cardboard Viewfinder
opening.need: the cardboard frame from last night · masking tape · 1 permanent marker.
steps: She holds the frame up to one eye and walks the room with it. Ask her what is inside the window and what got left out.
Tape a strip across the bottom of the frame and write THE FAMILY PHOTOGRAPHER on it in marker. Let her fill in one letter.
Ask her what she would keep out of this whole house. Take the first three answers and write nothing down. Tell her the camera is hers at 9:15.

main.title: Her Turn With the Camera
materials: 1 old phone or any digital camera (if you have neither, your own phone with the wrist strap round her wrist)
1 sheet of paper for her list of twelve
steps: Tape a strip of masking tape across the back of the camera and write her name on it in marker. If you are lending your own phone, wind the strap twice round her wrist and tape the loose end down.
Show her the button once, then take your hands off it. She lines each shot up through the cardboard frame first, drops the frame, and shoots.
Number the sheet of paper one to twelve. Twelve photographs of the things in this house she wants to keep.
After each one, ask why that. Write her answer on the numbered line word for word, wrong grammar and all.
Somewhere in the twelve every person in the house has to appear, you included. Stand where she puts you.
Go through all twelve on the screen at the end while she reads her own list back off your handwriting.
main.tip: Straighten nothing and move nothing out of shot. The dishwashing in the background is half of why the photograph will be worth having in ten years.

outside.title: Birds Carrying Breakfast
paras: Every bird on the street is running a delivery service this week. Stand still by a hedge and watch for one flying with a full beak, a grub or a worm or a lump of moss, and it never stops to eat any of it. Follow it and you find the nest. Take the camera and let her photograph the tree, even with no bird in it.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a second or two before he sits down hard. He wants the camera because you want the camera, so let Azlyn photograph him instead. Outside he points at whatever moves. Say the word for it once and leave a gap, because the naming lands better on a thing he chose to point at.

second.title: The World From Kreston's Height
second.intro: Six spots in the house, three heights at each, eighteen photographs. Kreston lives in a different version of this room.
materials: Masking tape, 6 pieces to mark the spots
steps: Walk the downstairs together and pick six spots: the kitchen doorway, under the table, the bottom stair, wherever she says. Press a piece of masking tape on the floor at each and number them one to six in marker.
Sit Kreston's toy on the floor at spot one. Kneel down and hold the camera at the height of his head for the first photograph.
Same tape, same spot, and she takes the second one standing at her own eye height.
For the third she stretches the camera as high as her arms go, or you lift her up and she shoots from there.
Work through all six spots that way. Tick each height off on the paper as you go, because eighteen photographs run together fast.
Sit down with the screen and give her three shots of one spot out of order. Let her say whose is whose before you tell her.
Hunt for the toy in all three. It fills the frame from Kreston's height and you can hardly find it from yours.
second.tip: Kneeling gets old by the third spot. Sit on the floor and let her be the one going up and down, and keep her thumb clear of the lens.

alternatives: Photograph one room from all four corners and pick the best.
Skip the heights and look through the twelve again on the sofa.
Draw the thing she photographed first, from memory.
Let her photograph the whole walk to the park and nothing indoors.
outAgain: Meet a friend at the park, and the camera comes
The park on your own if nobody is free by two
The playground, one photograph of every thing she climbs
The corner store for something for Sunday
The green with a ball and the camera left at home

aroundWorld.title: Mother's Day Everywhere 💐
paras: Mexico fixes its Día de las Madres to May 10 whatever weekday it lands on, and the day opens with a song sung at the bedroom door before breakfast. Thailand honors mothers in August, and children hand over garlands of jasmine. Ethiopian families keep Antrosht at the end of the rainy season: daughters bring vegetables and cheese, sons bring meat, and all of it goes into one hash cooked and eaten together.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Antrosht style, Azlyn picks every ingredient that goes on Sunday's cake and Joseph puts on every one of them.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Mexican schools close on May 10 even when it falls midweek.

days.krestonPM: Put him down on the grass at the park with the stroller brake on and stay at arm's reach. At 11 months he will haul himself up the fence rail, let go, stand for a beat, and drop. He does that twenty times in an hour.

insight.headline: Tools shape what a child notices.
paras: A camera puts a frame round the world, and a frame is an instruction to choose. Azlyn has walked past this kitchen every day of her life. Hand her something that takes one rectangle at a time and she starts hunting for what belongs inside it. A magnifying glass does the same thing to a paving slab, a flashlight does it to a cupboard, a jam jar does it to a puddle. The tool decides which question she asks. Twelve is a small enough number to hurt, so she has to leave things out. Read her twelve reasons back to her in December.

days.safety: Peel the six floor tapes up the moment you finish and count them. Masking tape is exactly what an 11-month-old puts in his mouth. The camera strap goes round her wrist, never her neck, and comes off before she runs.

days.title: The Questions at the Table
days.prepTonight: Get the big plate and five saucers onto a shelf she can reach, and put the plastic wrap and the thick card beside them.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Plate With Everybody On It

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: The Walk to Buy One Thing

opening.title: What Everybody Loves to Eat
steps: She goes round the house at breakfast with one question: what is your favorite thing to eat? Kreston gets asked too, and you answer for him out loud.
Write each answer down with the name beside it. Hand her the marker for the first letter of every name.
Read the list back and circle the ones already in the house. The uncircled one is what you walk to the store for at ten thirty.

main.title: The Plate With Everybody On It
materials: Foods from her morning list, out of the fridge and the cupboard
Card and 1 permanent marker for the folded name flags
Plastic wrap or a second plate to cover it
steps: Stand the big plate on the table and set the five saucers on it. Four are for the four of you, the fifth for whoever she decides is coming.
She fetches each circled food and puts it where she wants it. Anything round gets quartered lengthways with the blunt table knife first, your hand over hers on the handle.
One food per saucer, one person per saucer. The fifth holds something everybody in this house eats.
Fold pieces of card into standing flags. Write the names in marker, she copies a letter into each, one flag beside each saucer.
Cover it with plastic wrap or the second plate upside down, and put it on the middle shelf of the fridge.
She sets the rule out loud: nobody opens it once the last food goes on after the store walk, nobody looks, and she carries it out at six.
main.tip: Take her list at face value. Cold sausage next to raspberries is a correct answer to the question she asked.

outside.title: The Walk to Buy One Thing
paras: Walk to the store for the one uncircled thing and nothing else. Give her the coins before you go in and let her hand them over at the register. May mornings need one layer, and neither of you reached for the coats you fought about in March. She carries the bag home and straight to the fridge. She lifts the cover, sets the last food on its empty saucer and covers the plate again.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months. Sit him in the high chair at the table with a saucer of his own while she builds the big plate. He has started holding food out to you and snatching it back before you can take it, a joke he invented this month. Take the bait every time.

second.title: Everybody's Name on a Card
second.intro: She cannot read, so every card this afternoon has to work as a picture. Four questions for dinner and a name at every seat.
materials: Napkins, or squares of paper towels
The silverware and the plates for five
steps: Pick four questions with her for tonight: what made you laugh, what was the hard bit, what did you eat that you liked, who did you help.
Cut four pieces of card to fit her hand, using the adult scissors while she holds them flat.
Write one question on each in marker, then she draws a picture beside it so she knows which is which. A laughing mouth, a heavy rock, a plate.
Fold five more pieces of card in half so they stand up. One name on each in marker, and she covers the rest in crayon.
She practices reading her four pictures back to you. Let her get one wrong and leave it wrong.
Napkins folded her way, one per place.
Lay the table at two for six o'clock: plates, silverware, a name card at each seat, the four question cards stacked in the middle. Nobody eats there until dinner.
second.tip: Keep the tenth card back, because one always gets torn. Leave the table laid all afternoon where she walks past it.

alternatives: Name cards only, and skip the questions.
Draw everybody in the family instead, one card each.
Fold every napkin in the drawer a different way.
Let her decide where everyone sits and move the chairs.
outAgain: The pet store and the garden center, in that order, for the fish tanks first
The garden center alone if the pet store is packed
The park, and home by three thirty for the last hour in the yard
A drive to look at other people's front yards in bloom
days.krestonPM: He goes in the carrier facing out for the fish tanks. At 11 months a wall of moving light holds him longer than any toy in the store, so give him a full minute in front of one tank. Back home he sits under the laid table looking up at five chair legs.

insight.headline: One of the oldest child-centered teaching rituals we still have.
paras: At Passover, a few weeks back this spring, the youngest child at the table asks the Four Questions and the rest of the meal answers them. The tradition is getting on for two thousand years old and it is built around a child who asks. Azlyn asking four questions tonight sits in that line. She holds the floor, the table answers her, and a question of hers stops a room. Three-year-olds ask hundreds of questions a day and get most of them half-answered on the move. Keep the cards. Ask them again at Christmas, and again when she is seven, and listen to the answers change.

days.safety: Small round foods on an open plate with an 11-month-old at the table: grapes and cherry tomatoes quartered lengthways, no whole nuts, no olives with pits in, and nothing left within reach of the high chair. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Mother's Day
days.prepTonight: Joseph: the tray, the paint, the brush, the thick card and April's and January's handprint sheets off the wall and out on the counter tonight, and the sponge cake bought or baked and hidden.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Card That Gets Made Every May

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Story of the Night She Was Born

opening.title: The Tray She Carries In
opening.need: 1 tray · breakfast · 1 sheet of paper · 1 pen.
steps: Azlyn carries the tray in with both hands and Joseph carries anything hot behind her. She puts it down wherever it lands.

Six questions. She asks, you answer out loud: your favorite thing this year, the funniest thing Azlyn has said, the best day, one thing you want before next May, what Kreston did that you want to remember, and one thing you would tell yourself last May.
Joseph writes the six answers down word for word and props the paper where nobody moves it. They go on the card at 9:15.

main.title: The Card That Gets Made Every May
materials: 1 sheet of thick card, letter size or bigger
1 shallow bowl of warm water and 2 washcloths
The six answers from the breakfast tray
April's and January's handprint sheets, to hold up beside it
steps: Paint Azlyn's palm with the brush rather than dipping her hand. Press flat on the left of the card, count to three, lift straight up. Hand into the bowl, dry on the first washcloth.
Kreston next, while he is calm and pinned across a knee. His hand is a fist at 11 months, so open it flat, press it down fast, and take whatever smear comes out. Second washcloth.
Pencil the date and both names underneath, then go over the pencil in marker once it is dry. Write May, her 3 and his 11 months beside the pair.
Copy the six answers onto the card in marker, in Brooklyn's exact words. Do not shorten the funny one.
Hold April's sheet up beside today's, then January's under both. Three of the five months so far, side by side. Let Azlyn put her hand on all three.
All three go back on the wall where the others are. This one is May, fifth of twelve. If you are marking the door frame this month, the pencil is already out and this is the afternoon for it.
main.tip: Do Kreston first if he is asleep and Azlyn first if he is not. Have the washcloth in your hand before the paint touches anyone.

outside.title: The Bunch She Picks Herself
paras: Walk the roadsides and let her pick dandelions, violets, clover and the buttercups along the edge of any grass nobody mows. Nothing out of a garden that is not yours. She will pick every stem too short for a vase, so take a jam jar and let the bunch be the wrong shape.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and everything he holds goes to his mouth, so his flowers stay in your hand and his job is smelling them. Hold one under his nose and watch his whole face change. Name it for him once, and let the noise he makes back at the dandelion stand as his answer.

second.title: The Cake She Ices Herself
second.intro: Hand this page to Joseph. Both children go into the kitchen, the door shuts, and Brooklyn does not come in for ninety minutes.
materials: 1 plain sponge or a store-bought loaf cake (plain cookies work the same way)
steps: Powdered sugar into the bowl. Azlyn tips it and half of it goes on the counter.
Water in one spoonful at a time while she stirs. Stop when it falls off the spoon in a ribbon and holds its shape for a second.
Food coloring, one drop, her choice of color, and she stirs it through. Two drops if the first disappoints her.
Stand the cake on the plate. She spreads the icing with the butter knife, thick in some places and bare in others, and nobody smooths it after her.
Sprinkles or chopped fruit go on by the fistful. Do not ration or arrange them.
Twenty minutes for the icing to set. She washes the bowl and the spoon in the sink while it does.
She carries it out on the plate when she can no longer stand waiting.
second.tip: Keep a couple of spoonfuls of powdered sugar back in the bag. A spoonful stirred in fixes any mix that has gone too runny.

alternatives: Ice plain cookies, one each, and skip the cake.
Make a card for Brooklyn's own mother and post it tomorrow.
Bunch the flowers into three jars for three windowsills.
Let Azlyn dictate a letter to Brooklyn while Joseph writes it down.
outAgain: A long walk with the stroller, and Brooklyn picks the route for once
The woods, for the last of the spring wildflowers before the canopy shuts
A café with outdoor tables and a slow hour
The long way round to somewhere with a view
Nowhere. The garden, a blanket and the flowers in the jar
days.krestonPM: He goes in the stroller for the long walk and stays awake for most of it at 11 months. Stop somewhere with grass and stand him up holding the stroller handle for a few minutes. Point out what Azlyn is doing and name it, because he watches her more than he watches either of you.

insight.headline: Rituals that repeat annually do something one-off events can't.
paras: Azlyn has no working idea of how long a year is. A thing that happens once a year, remembered from last time and expected next time, is how a year turns into a real unit for her: the handprint card, the same walk, the capsule on the shelf. The second time is when it starts working, and the fifth time it belongs to her rather than to you. Keep this one small enough to survive a bad May. One sheet of card, two hands and six answers takes forty minutes, and forty minutes is a tradition you can still manage in 2031.

days.safety: Two roadside plants are out now, both dangerous. Poison hemlock stands waist-high, lacy white heads on a purple-blotched stem, every part of it deadly. Wild parsnip has flat yellow heads and sap that burns skin in sunlight. Nothing tall, white or lacy gets picked, and both of you wash your hands before lunch. Nothing goes in Kreston's mouth or hands. Washable non-toxic paint only, and the washcloth is in your hand before the paint touches him.

days.title: The Button Tin
days.prepTonight: Tip the button tin and the odds-and-ends drawer into one jar, leaving out anything sharp and anything with a point on it. Stand it out of Kreston's reach overnight, with a bath towel folded flat beside it.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Box of Things Nobody Throws Away

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Keepsake Box on Her Own

opening.title: Everything Out on the Towel
opening.need: the jar of odds and ends · 1 bath towel · a table she has to stand up at.
steps: Towel flat on the table first. It stops everything rolling and quiets the pouring.
Tip the jar out in the middle and sit down opposite her. Say nothing for two minutes while she goes through it.
Ask her to find two that are exactly the same, and take her word for it whatever she holds up.

main.title: The Twins in the Tin
materials: The button tin, or a jar of odds and ends: bottle caps, coins, keys, corks, lids, clothespins, spoons, fabric scraps
2 saucers or small bowls, one for the pairs and one for the singles
1 tray for the row at the end
steps: Clear a strip down the middle of the towel and give her one rule: two things the same in every way go in the strip, and the rest stay put.
She works the tin on her own. Keep your hands off, including the pair you can see from where you sit.

Once she slows, hand her the near misses: two buttons the same size in different colors, a big key and a small one, a clothespin with a spring and one without. She rules on each and you write the reason down.
Count the pairs into one saucer, two at a time, out loud, then the singles into the other. There are far more singles than she expects.
Tip the singles back out and let her choose six for the tray: the six things in this house that nothing else matches.
The rest goes back in the tin. The tray of six stays for the day, because the shoebox at one o'clock runs on the same idea.
main.tip: Take her word for the same, then ask what makes them the same. Two red buttons with a different number of holes last about a minute of that.

outside.title: The Leaves Over the Path
paras: Walk the January route as far as the trees along the path. They are in full leaf now and the shape she looked at in the frost has gone. Stand her in the same spot and ask what happened. Take her theory, and pick one leaf for the box.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months. Sit him on the floor away from the table with a wooden spoon and a metal one, and let him find out that the two sound different against the floorboards. He bangs them together, drops one, and looks at you to see whether that was interesting. Say what he did back to him.

second.title: The Box of Things Nobody Throws Away
second.intro: Five things out of this house nobody would ever throw out, and a story for each. Brooklyn picks them.
materials: 5 real objects with a story attached, chosen by Brooklyn
The leaf from this morning's walk
steps: Walk the house on your own after lunch and pick five: a ring, a ticket, a baby hat, a spoon off your grandmother's table, anything with somebody in it.
Take them one at a time. She holds each one and says how it feels: cold, heavy, soft, worn smooth.
Tell the story. Keep it to a minute and do not tidy it up. The sad ones are the ones she asks about again.
She asks one question about each. Write her question and your answer on a scrap of paper and tape it on.
She draws all five on one sheet with the crayons, or whichever she liked best. The drawing goes in the box.
Add the photo and today's leaf. Lid on, and write THINGS NOBODY THROWS AWAY across it with the date underneath.
Put the box on a shelf she can reach. She goes back into it at quarter past four unasked.
second.tip: Pick one object that belonged to somebody she never met. She will ask the same three questions about it for a year.

alternatives: One object and one story, then out to the yard.
Sort the button tin by color instead and photograph the rows.
Let her fill a box with five things of her own choosing.
outAgain: The woods loop, and every tree is doing what this morning's tree did
The riverside path if the woods are still wet underfoot
The park, for running rather than looking at anything
A walk to post the card to Brooklyn's mother
days.krestonPM: Take him out of the stroller in the woods and set him on his feet in the leaf litter, holding your two fingers. At 11 months uneven ground is a whole workout, and he lifts his knees high over roots that are barely there.

insight.headline: "Same" is a harder word than it looks.
paras: The word does most of its work for Azlyn as the same in the way I happen to be looking right now. Two red buttons match until somebody counts the holes, and then they do not. Holding two objects side by side and running down size and color and weight and shape is slow work at three, and she calls a match on the first thing that lines up. Asking what makes them the same forces the second look, and the second look is the skill. She finds far fewer real pairs than she expects, and the six leftovers stand on the tray all day as the proof.

days.safety: Buttons, coins, keys and bottle caps are all choke-sized and Kreston is pulling to stand at table height. Work on a raised table, count them back into the tin before he is on the floor, and shake the towel out over the tin so nothing is left on the carpet under it. The tray of six goes up out of his reach whenever she leaves the table, and comes down when she asks for it. The keepsake box goes on a shelf she can reach and he cannot, and the lid stays on when she is not in it.

days.title: Nothing in the Bin
days.prepTonight: Go through the fridge before bed and move anything on its last day to the front of the middle shelf, at her eye level for the morning.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: The Mended Toy Goes to Bed

opening.title: What Needs Eating First
steps: Open the fridge together and take everything off the front of the middle shelf. She carries them to the tray one at a time.
She bends every carrot and presses every tomato. Tired, or fine? Her call, and she is a harsher judge than you.
Write the tired ones on the paper in marker. That list is lunch, snack and dinner, and nothing on it goes in the bin.

main.title: The Use-It-Up Fritters
materials: Whatever needs eating: a tired carrot, a zucchini, a cooked potato, the last of the cheese, soft herbs
A splash of milk and a pinch of salt
1 bowl, 1 fork, 1 grater (adult only), 1 frying pan, 1 spatula, paper towels
steps: You grate everything into the bowl, carrot and zucchini and potato and cheese, while she reads the next thing off her list.
She squeezes the grated zucchini over the sink with both fists until the water stops coming. Wet mix makes fritters that fall apart.
She cracks the egg into the bowl and fishes the shell out with her fingers. Herbs torn in by hand.
Four heaped spoons of flour, a splash of milk, a pinch of salt, and she beats it with the fork until it holds in a lump on the tines.
Kreston out of the kitchen. Oil into the pan on a medium heat, pan handle turned inward, and cook fork-loads flattened into rounds, three minutes a side, turning them with the spatula.
Onto folded paper towels away from the heat. She counts them out loud. Half get eaten at quarter past ten, half go cold for dinner.
main.tip: Cook one on its own first and eat it standing up. If it falls apart, another spoon of flour into the bowl fixes the rest.

outside.title: The Puddle That Shrank
paras: Find a puddle left from the last rain and lay a ring of stones round its edge. Go on with the walk, and come back past it on the way home. In May sun the ring is a size too big by lunchtime. Ask her where the water went and take her theory, however wrong.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and eats what everybody else eats now. Break him a cooled fritter into finger-length strips and let him feed himself. He will hold your eye, say something at the plate, and hold his hand out for more. Answer that noise as if it were a word.

second.title: The Mending Pile
second.intro: The bottom of the closet has been collecting torn things since March. This afternoon they get fixed, and she does the pulling.
materials: 2–3 torn things out of the mending pile, and 1 soft toy with a split seam
1 large blunt darning needle (fabric glue or an iron-on patch does the same job with no needle in the house)
1 scrap of fabric for a patch
steps: Tip the pile onto the floor and let her choose three. The soft toy with the split seam goes first, because it has a name and a bedtime.
Cut an arm's length of wool with the scissors. Hold the needle steady while she pushes the wool through the eye. It takes six goes.
Sew the seam with big loose stitches. You push the needle through from your side, she pulls it out on hers.
Buttons next, one at a time. Hold each flat on the fabric while she pulls the wool through the holes four times.
Patch the biggest hole: fabric scrap over it, her thumbs holding it flat, big stitches round the edge.
Cut the wool and tie it off. Let her hold a finger on the knot while you pull it tight.
She folds the mended things and puts each back where it came from. The toy comes upstairs at bedtime.
second.tip: Sew badly on purpose. Stitches she can see are stitches she knows she made.

alternatives: Iron-on patches only, no needle in the house.
Sew buttons onto a scrap of fabric for practice and mend nothing.
Wash and dry the soft toy instead, and hang it on the line by its ears.
outAgain: Swimming
The pool's quiet hour if the after-school crowd is in
Indoor playground if the pool is shut
The park on the way home to dry her hair off
days.krestonPM: Kreston is 11 months and holds the pool rail while you keep both hands on him. Walk him along the wall in the shallow end and let him slap the water. Twenty minutes, then out and dressed before he goes cold. He loses heat faster than she does.

insight.headline: "Waste" is a concept, and it's teachable through objects.
paras: Azlyn cannot hold an argument about food waste. She can hold a bendy carrot that turned into lunch, and a teddy with a split seam that went to bed mended. The idea arrives through her hands: a thing that looked finished had one more use in it, and somebody in this house is the person who finds that use. Say the reason out loud once while your hands are busy, then let the carrot do the rest of the talking. Do this often enough at three and it lands as a fact about how her family behaves. She will be checking the fridge before you do inside a year.

days.safety: Hot oil in a shallow pan with an 11-month-old cruising the kitchen units: pan handle turned in, Kreston out of the kitchen while it is on the heat, and the pan left to go cold at the back of the counter. The grater and the scissors stay in your hand. The needle is a large blunt darning needle and it only ever moves between your hand and hers, never onto the table, and it goes back in the tin the second you stop. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: The Big Sister
days.prepTonight: Wash a plastic bottle with its screw lid, an empty wipes tub and a cardboard tube and leave them draining, with the rice and the packing tape beside them.

schedule.label: Wind-Down
schedule.name: Reading What She Chose at the Library

opening.title: The Table With No Instructions
opening.need: the washed bottle, tub and tube · the rice · the ribbon · Kreston on the floor where she can see him.
steps: Lay it out in a row before she sits down and put nothing else on the table.
Tell her one thing and stop: today she is making a toy for Kreston, and this is everything there is. Offer no ideas, not even when she asks.
Sit down with your coffee and let her handle everything. She picks things up and puts them down for ten minutes.

main.title: A Present for Kreston
materials: 1 clean plastic bottle with a screw lid
Ribbon or fabric strips, none longer than a hand's width
steps: Give her the three tests and hold her to them: too big to swallow, nothing that pulls off, and it does something when he shakes it.
She pours rice into the bottle, a third full. Screw the lid down hard and wrap packing tape round the neck and over the lid five or six times so it cannot come off in his mouth.
Shake test. If it makes no noise, more rice. If it makes a dull thud, less.
Cut the ribbon into strips with the adult scissors, none longer than her hand is wide. She threads one through the wipes tub lid and you tape the end inside so it cannot be pulled out.
Post everything she has made through the cardboard tube. Anything that drops through is small enough to choke him and stays off the floor today.
She writes his name on the bottle in marker, or her version of it. Put it in his hands and watch.
main.tip: Let the toy be ugly. Her design, her tape, her amount of rice. What he loves is that it is loud and new.

outside.title: Grass Under His Feet
paras: Warm enough now to take Kreston's shoes and socks off outside. Stand him barefoot on the lawn or the park grass with Azlyn holding both his hands, and watch him refuse to put his heels down. Give her the job of walking him four steps.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months and stands alone for a few seconds at a time. Grass is a new surface, so he grips with his toes and freezes. Sit a foot away and let him come to you. Azlyn's hands are the safety net.

second.title: Everything He's Allowed to Chew
second.intro: Kreston gets a basket of real household things instead of toys, and Azlyn finds out which ones he wants.
materials: 11 household objects: wooden spoon, metal tablespoon, small saucepan lid, silicone spatula, hairbrush, washcloth, cotton scarf, metal measuring cup, small mixing bowl, tea strainer, wooden coaster
steps: She goes round the house collecting and you hold the veto. This morning's rule applies: too big to swallow, nothing that comes apart in his mouth.
Everything goes in the soapy water and she washes each one, hand-hot. She scrubs the tea strainer and the hairbrush hardest.
Lay them on the dish towel to dry while she names each one out loud.
Into the basket, basket onto the floor, and both of you sit down beside it with Kreston.
Hand him nothing. He chooses, and Azlyn calls out the name of whatever he picks up.
Watch what he does with each: bangs it, mouths it, passes it hand to hand, drops it over the side to see where it goes.
The three he keeps coming back to stay in the basket by the sofa and the rest go back to the kitchen. Azlyn decides which three.
second.tip: The metal spoon and the saucepan lid beat every plastic toy in this house. Anything that goes in his mouth comes back to the soapy water before the drawer.

alternatives: Five objects instead of eleven, on the kitchen floor.
Fill the wipes tub with scarves for him to pull out.
Let her build a tower for him to knock over, twenty times.
outAgain: The library, and she chooses one book for herself and one for Kreston
The board-book corner and nothing else if he is fractious
Indoor playground if the library is packed with a school group
The park on the walk home, for the swings
days.krestonPM: Put him down in the board-book corner and let him chew whatever he gets hold of. At 11 months he cruises the low shelving and pulls everything off it, so pick the aisle you mind reshelving least. Let Azlyn carry his book to the desk.

insight.headline: Abundance of choice produces better work than the perfect kit.
paras: A craft kit has one outcome in the box and her job is to arrive at it. A table of odds and ends has no outcome in it at all, so she has to invent one. She spent ten minutes this morning touching things and picking nothing, which looked like being stuck and was her working through the options. Give her more materials than the job needs and no picture of the finished thing. The toy she handed her brother came out of a decision she made on her own, and she will give it to him again tomorrow to watch it work twice.

days.safety: Everything going near Kreston today is homemade, so you check it and not her: the bottle lid taped shut with packing tape so no rice escapes, nothing that fits through the cardboard tube, no ribbon or string longer than a hand's width, no batteries, and no chipped or sharp rims. He never has any of it out of your sight. The washing water is hand-hot and stays up on the counter, out of his reach, and gets poured away as soon as the last thing is washed. The scissors stay with you.

days.title: Jobs That Need Muscles
days.prepTonight: Put a wash on before bed and set the finish time for eight in the morning. Drop the clothesline to her height while there is still light.

schedule.label: The Main Event
schedule.name: The Wet Basket and the Line

opening.title: Pulling the Sheets Off
opening.need: every bed in the house · 1 laundry basket · laundry detergent.
steps: She strips the beds and you follow her round. Pillowcases she does on her own; for the duvet cover she takes two corners and walks backwards while you hold the other end.
Everything into the basket, and she drags it down the hall.
Leave the basket by the machine. She scoops the powder into the drawer and the sheets go in after the overnight wash comes out at 9:15.

main.title: The Wet Basket and the Line
materials: The overnight wash, still in the machine
1 clothespin bag with 30 clothespins or more
A clothesline dropped low, or a clothes airer she can reach over
steps: She opens the machine and hauls the wet wash into the basket a piece at a time. Wet cotton is four times the weight of dry.
She drags the full basket out to the line. Do not carry it for her and do not take half out.
Sort on the ground into two piles, big and small. Small things are hers alone: socks, underwear, washcloths, Kreston's undershirts.
Hang the clothespin bag on the line within her reach. Two clothespins per thing, and crooked stays crooked all day.
Big things together: you hold the sheet up off the grass, she clips the corners, and she goes up the step stool for the far end.
Load the stripped sheets in and set the machine going. Send her out at four to feel whether the line has gone dry.
main.tip: This is the first week of the year the sun will dry a full line before dinner, so say that out loud when she checks at four.

outside.title: Two Full Watering Cans
paras: Everything planted in April wants water this week. Fill the can to the top and let her carry it. She manages about six steps before she has to put it down and pick it up again. Two full cans, poured on the roots and not the leaves. Her arms will ache and she will want to do a third.

days.infant: Kreston is 11 months. Empty the laundry basket and give it to him on the grass to push, because it slides enough to hold him up and not enough to shoot away. He will walk the length of the garden behind it. Keep the clothespins off the ground while he is down there.

second.title: Clean Sheets on Every Bed
second.intro: Clean dry sheets out of the cupboard and onto every bed in this house, and she makes all of them.
materials: Clean dry sheets, duvet covers and pillowcases for every bed
One belonging per person to go back on their bed
steps: Load the basket at the cupboard, one full set per bed, and she drags it room to room and unloads it.
Fitted sheet first. You take two corners, she takes the two opposite, and she pulls hers down over the mattress corners. One will ping off. Do it again without a word.
Duvet cover next, and she climbs inside it to hold the two far corners while you shake it down over the duvet. Best ten seconds of her day.
Pillowcases are hers alone. Stand the pillow on its end on the floor and pull the case down over it like a sock.
She smooths the whole bed flat with both hands, wall side first, leaning right across to reach.
One belonging goes back onto each bed: a book on yours, the mended toy from Tuesday on hers, a muslin on Kreston's.
She walks you round all the beds at the end.
second.tip: Take the beds in her order, hers last. She works harder on the others when she knows her own is still to come.

alternatives: Her bed only, and leave the rest for tomorrow.
Fold the dry laundry off the line into piles by person.
Build a den out of the clean sheets before they go on.
Match every sock in the basket, out loud, in pairs.
outAgain: The market, and she carries her own bag round it
The produce market alone if the market has packed up early
The bakery, and she chooses what goes with tonight
The park on the way home to spend what is left
The thrift store, to look at other people's spoons and buttons
days.krestonPM: Market stalls are at his eye level from the carrier, so face him out and stop at the fruit. At 11 months he grabs what he can reach, so keep him an arm's length off the display and hand him something he is allowed to hold. Let Azlyn choose one thing for him to try at dinner.

insight.headline: Heavy work is the most reliable regulation tool you have.
paras: Dragging a wet basket, hauling a watering can and shoving a loaded pillow into a case all send steady pressure through her muscles and joints, and you can watch that pressure take the edge off her. It reads the same way on the wound-up three-year-old and on the floppy whiny one, which is what makes it worth building into a day before things go wrong. Put the carrying jobs before the parts of the day that tend to fall apart. Ten minutes of it buys you the hour after it. Laundry, water and shopping bags are free, endless, and she gets to be the one the house needed.

days.safety: Laundry pods look like candy and burn a child's mouth and eyes. They stay shut in a high cupboard and she scoops powder instead. Keep the airer away from where Kreston is pulling to stand, because a loaded one tips onto a baby, and check the clothespins are off the floor before he is down.
